Problems found by handling, testing and flying the hardware.** Problems become visible when people work with the physical hardware: technicians who notice that a material is wrong or a tile moves too much, and test failures and post-flight inspections that reveal what the design did not anticipate. Once found, a problem is chased and fixed, and the other vehicles are checked. Concepts: C01, C02. 55 primary passages from 6 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Smith, Thomas, White). **T02. Problems that stay out of sight.** Problems no one could see in time: supplier and sub-tier changes made without anyone knowing, failure modes and consequences no one understood or could observe (no instrumentation, no view of the vehicle in flight, no way to inspect foam), and requirements met only on paper, found after Challenger to have been ‘certified by analysis’. Concepts: C04, C05, C06. 57 primary passages from 6 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Smith, Thomas, White). ### D2. Moving concerns to where they can be acted on Once someone has a concern, it has to reach a person or body that can act. Informants describe concerns stalling at organizational lines, individuals stating their own judgment against the line of authority at some personal cost, and the technical depth and physical closeness that let concerns move faster. *3 themes, 9 concepts, 143 primary passages; informants: Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Smith, Thomas, White.* **T03. Concerns stalled at organizational lines.** Concerns that cross a boundary — between contractor and program, between projects or Centers, between designers and the launch site, between customer and contractor — move slowly or not at all. It takes months of data to get the program to own a problem; projects deny a problem is theirs; designers leave the consequences to the Cape; contractors act ahead of, or resist, NASA involvement. Concepts: C07, C12, C13, C24. 59 primary passages from 6 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Smith, Thomas, White). **T04. Personal judgment against the line of authority.** Individuals stating their own technical view when it departs from the official position or from senior people, and the shaping of what is reported upward. Informants describe being asked for their own opinion, open technical argument, briefing charts reworked by superiors, and the personal stakes of owning or reporting a problem. C09 rests on Smith alone. Concepts: C08, C09, C10. 47 primary passages from 5 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Smith, White). **T05. Technical depth and proximity that let concerns travel.** Conditions informants credit with getting problems raised and handled: government engineers deep enough to challenge contractors, open forums where people were encouraged to ask questions, and experts placed next to the hardware and to each other so that issues are handled quickly. Concepts: C11, C14. 37 primary passages from 6 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Smith, Thomas, White). ### D3. Closing technical questions How a concern was brought to a decision. Informants describe evidence and outside expertise as the arbiter, formal machinery and decision rights, flying with problems not fully resolved, the opposite move of adding protection beyond what evidence requires, the weight of committing to fly, and the schedule, money and end-of-program pressures bearing on all of these. *6 themes, 15 concepts, 386 primary passages; informants: Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Singer, Smith, Thomas, White.* **T06. Settling by evidence and outside expertise.** Questions and disagreements are settled by producing evidence: tests that ‘referee’ competing designs, systematic tracing of every possible cause, on-the-spot engineering problem-solving after a surprise, and bringing in parallel teams and outside experts. Concepts: C15, C16, C25, C28. 144 primary passages from 7 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Singer, Smith, Thomas, White). **T07. Formal closure and decision rights.** The formal channels that capture and close concerns (review item discrepancies, material review boards, certification and flight readiness reviews, launch-day polling) and where the authority to decide sits: the project manager's final vote or signature, reliance on experts, and the floor supervisor for whom analysis happens ‘a few levels above me’. Concepts: C21, C22. 59 primary passages from 7 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Singer, Smith, Thomas, White). **T08. Carrying the weight of committing to fly.** What committing to fly felt like to the people who signed off: a solid rocket motor that ‘can’t be tested’ before it carries a crew, ‘seven lives are riding on us’, lying awake over whether both boosters would light, and lasting apprehension at the moment Challenger was lost. Mostly post-Challenger. A single-concept theme: after the merge in T09, nothing else here shares this felt side of the decision. Concepts: C35. 16 primary passages from 5 informants (Mitchell, Sheehan, Singer, Smith, Thomas). **T09. Flying with problems not fully resolved.** Continuing to fly while a known problem is not fully resolved, by one of four routes: reclassifying it as maintenance rather than flight safety (C03), deciding to fly on a ‘most-probable cause’, a worst-case test or a partial repair (C17), containing it with workarounds, operating limits and repeated inspections (C18), or giving up margin for weight (C20). C20 rests on Pessin alone. Concepts: C03, C17, C18, C20. 86 primary passages from 6 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Singer, Smith, Thomas, White). **T10. Erring toward protection.** Resolving a problem by adding protection beyond what the evidence requires: redundancy and margin added when harm could not be proven or disproven, built designs rejected as not safe enough, and designs chosen to keep debris and damage away from the Orbiter. Mostly the post-Challenger redesign, with debris concerns before Challenger and after Columbia. Concepts: C19, C37. 29 primary passages from 7 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Singer, Smith, Thomas, White). **T11. Schedule, money and the program's end.** Pressures that bear on how and when questions are closed: schedule contingency removed, hardware committed before tests, budgets cut, timelines everyone knew were unachievable, and, late in the program, whether a fix could even be incorporated before the last flight. Concepts: C23, C34. 52 primary passages from 7 informants (Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Singer, Smith, Thomas, White). ### D4. Resetting after the accidents What informants say each accident changed in concern handling. After Challenger: outside eyes on the program, new people and repaired relations, and a swing toward caution and paperwork that was later pulled back. After Columbia: accepted explanations had to be demonstrated, and concrete criteria tightened. *4 themes, 8 concepts, 127 primary passages; informants: Mitchell, Pessin, Sheehan, Singer, Smith, Thomas, White.* **T12. Outside eyes after Challenger.** Requirements imposed by the accident commission and new leadership, formal oversight panels, astronauts in reviews, independent safety and quality, and scrutiny from Congress, the press and investigators. Almost entirely the solid rocket motor redesign; C26 rests almost entirely on Mitchell. Concepts: C26, C27, C36. 52 primary passages from 3 informants (Mitchell, Smith, Thomas). **T13. Replacing people and repairing relations after Challenger.** Leadership replaced by people not on the project at the time of the accident, devastated morale, and deliberate work to end blame between NASA and the contractor and build one team. Concepts: C29. 19 primary passages from 3 informants (Mitchell, Smith, Thomas). **T14. Over-correction and pull-back after Challenger.** After Challenger, concern-raising and paperwork multiplied (thousands of review items, an ‘overzealous’ processing team, repair records from 3 pages to 21) and control moved from the shop to engineering; managers and the shop later pushed back to restore pace. Concepts: C30, C31. 27 primary passages from 5 informants (Pessin, Sheehan, Smith, Thomas, White). **T15. From acceptance to demonstration after Columbia.** After Columbia, explanations and requirements were no longer taken on trust and had to be demonstrated, and repair, inspection and imaging criteria tightened. C32 rests on Singer alone; C33 is mostly White. Concepts: C32, C33. 29 primary passages from 3 informants (Pessin, Singer, White). ## Notes on the structure - Blind theme check (tools/compare_structures.py; _audit/blind_themes.json): a separate analyst grouped the 37 concepts from labels and definitions only. C21's quotes are about where decisions land (‘I had the final vote’, signing changes); C22's about disposition and clearance before flight, though a RID is also ‘a concern that somebody has raised’, so the machinery carries concerns as well as closing them; C28's about outside expertise used to correct problems and triage proposals; C35's about the weight of committing to fly. - Disagreement 4 (C03, C17, C18 as one theme): adopted. Their quotes share flying while a problem is not fully resolved — by reclassifying it, deciding under uncertainty, or containing it. T09 now holds C03, C17, C18 and C20; T08 keeps C35 alone. - Disagreement 2 (T04 split three ways) left as is: C08, C09 and C10 all concern an individual's position against the line of authority — stating one's own view, having one's reporting reshaped from above, and the personal exposure of doing so. - Disagreement 3 (C14 grouped with organizational distance; C11 with challenge) left as is: C11 and C14 describe conditions informants credit with letting concerns travel (technical depth, physical closeness), which is a different claim from the stalls at boundaries in T03. - Disagreement 5 (C20 with schedule and program pressure) left as is: C20's quotes are deliberate engineering trades of margin for weight, accepted as tolerable, not pressure from outside the engineering decision. - Disagreement 6 (C16 with problem detection) left as is: C16's quotes describe working out a fix after a problem is already known (‘Okay, where do we go from here?’), which is settling rather than surfacing.

## The model: a recurring cycle for handling concerns, reset twice

- **The cycle (every period):** a problem surfaces (D1), the concern moves to someone who can act (D2), and the question is closed (D3).
- **Two ways out of closure:**
  - a **learning loop**: fix it, carry the fix across the fleet, find the next problem;
  - a **drift loop**: accommodate it, and it drops out of view as a safety issue.
- **Four conditions** speed or divert the cycle: organizational lines, pressure, technical depth and proximity, and individual judgment.
- **Challenger** reset the cycle for the failed element: outside eyes, new people, a sharper sense of the weight of flying, and over-correction followed by pull-back. The reset stayed close to the solid rocket motor.
- **Columbia** changed the standard of proof, from acceptance to demonstration. Late in the program, the coming end of flights pushed decisions back toward containment.
- **In short:** Challenger mainly changed who looks at a problem and who decides; Columbia changed what counts as enough to fly.

# Grounded model: A recurring concern-handling cycle, reset twice

Stage 4 of the study (Gioia, Corley, & Hamilton, 2013, p. 22). Generated by
`tools/build_model.py` from `model.json`, `structure.json`, `concepts.json`
and the coded passages; edit those, not this file.

The model relates the themes and dimensions of `DATA_STRUCTURE.md` to one
another and over time. Each proposition names the themes it links and the
passages that support it. Every passage is checked against its transcript
lines and must belong, through its primary or secondary concept, to one of
the linked themes. Each proposition ends with a note on where its evidence
is thin. The literature has not yet been consulted.

## The model in brief

In every period the informants describe the same cycle: a problem surfaces (D1), a concern has to move to someone who can act on it (D2), and the question is closed (D3).

Closure goes one of two ways. Fixing a problem — by evidence, or by adding protection — feeds a learning loop: the hardware keeps revealing new problems and fixes are carried across the fleet. Accommodating a problem — reclassifying it, deciding on incomplete evidence, containing it, trading margin — feeds a drift loop: the problem stays in service and drops out of view as a safety issue.

Four conditions speed or divert the cycle: organizational lines slow, disown or defer concerns; schedule and budget pressure pushes closure ahead of evidence; technical depth and proximity speed concerns toward closure; and individual judgment changes a decision mainly when someone senior asks for it, at a personal cost.

Challenger reset the cycle for the failed element: outside eyes, new people and a new contractor relationship pushed closure toward test evidence and protection, made the weight of committing to fly sharper, and briefly overloaded the formal channels before managers and the shop pulled back. The reset stayed close to the solid rocket motor; between the accidents, accommodation persisted at boundaries elsewhere, notably debris.

Columbia changed the standard of proof — from accepting that an element had done its homework to asking it to demonstrate — and tightened criteria and visibility. Late in the program, the coming end of flights steered closure back toward containment, with changes reserved for safety.

In short: Challenger mainly changed who looks and who decides; Columbia mainly changed what counts as enough.

# Grounded model: A recurring concern-handling cycle, reset twice

Stage 4 of the study (Gioia, Corley, & Hamilton, 2013, p. 22). Generated by
`tools/build_model.py` from `model.json`, `structure.json`, `concepts.json`
and the coded passages; edit those, not this file.

The model relates the themes and dimensions of `DATA_STRUCTURE.md` to one
another and over time. Each proposition names the themes it links and the
passages that support it. Every passage is checked against its transcript
lines and must belong, through its primary or secondary concept, to one of
the linked themes. Each proposition ends with a note on where its evidence
is thin. The literature has not yet been consulted.

## The model in brief

In every period the informants describe the same cycle: a problem surfaces (D1), a concern has to move to someone who can act on it (D2), and the question is closed (D3).

Closure goes one of two ways. Fixing a problem — by evidence, or by adding protection — feeds a learning loop: the hardware keeps revealing new problems and fixes are carried across the fleet (P1). Accommodating a problem — reclassifying it, deciding on incomplete evidence, containing it, trading margin — keeps it in service; tentatively, and on hindsight-based evidence, it also drops out of view as a safety issue (P3, a drift loop).

Four conditions speed or divert the cycle: organizational lines slow, disown or defer concerns (P2); schedule and budget pressure pushes closure ahead of evidence (P4); technical depth and proximity speed concerns toward closure (P5); and individual judgment changes a decision mainly when someone senior asks for it, at a personal cost (P6).

Challenger reset the cycle for the failed element: outside eyes pushed closure toward test evidence and protection (P7); new leaders and a team moved into the contractor's plant changed the working relationship (P8); the swing to caution overloaded the formal channels before managers and the shop pulled back (P9); and committing to fly felt heavier (P10). Tentatively, the reset stayed close to the solid rocket motor, and between the accidents debris crossing element lines was still accommodated (P11).

Tentatively, Columbia changed the standard of proof — from accepting that an element had done its homework to asking it to demonstrate — and tightened criteria and visibility (P12); and in the last years the coming end of flights steered closure back toward containment, with changes reserved for safety (P13).

Our interpretation, not a claim any informant makes: Challenger mainly changed who looks and who decides; Columbia mainly changed what counts as enough (P14).

### P1. Learning loop

**Proposition.** Problems that surface in the hardware itself are usually chased to a cause and fixed, and the fix is carried to the other vehicles; this loop is how most problems informants describe were closed.

**Links.** T01 Problems found by handling, testing and flying the hardware → T06 Settling by evidence and outside expertise.

**Evidence.** 8 passages from 4 informants (White 4, Smith 2, Pessin 1, Sheehan 1); 8 first-hand; eras: pre-Challenger 6, between accidents 2.

- [WHI054] “Well, turns out we had some tiles still to replace when we found out that the heat sink underneath was soft. It should not be soft. It should be a hardness of at least forty, and this was less than fifteen. So anytime we find an issue, then we start taking off around it. We have to bound it, see how far it goes.” — White, `whitetr-7-12-11.txt` l. 1121–1127 (pre-Challenger)
- [WHI055] “Well, we removed more and found out they were still soft. So the Materials and Processes folks, the M&P engineers, went out and that’s what they discovered; the waterproofing was having this effect on the heat sink.” — White, `whitetr-7-12-11.txt` l. 1127–1131 (pre-Challenger)
- [WHI056] “So we started chasing this. When we got done chasing all of these issues, we had removed a little over 4,000 tile.” — White, `whitetr-7-12-11.txt` l. 1133–1135 (pre-Challenger)
- [PES016] “Martin placed an order and the shipping paper was fine, cans were labeled properly, the very very preliminary test that’s done at receiving said the material was fine, and it was released to the floor. The technician sprayed the 1,000-square-foot dome and said, “This isn’t the same stuff I’ve been spraying.” I think he got a bonus for reporting it, hopefully he did.” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 968–978 (pre-Challenger)
- [SMI015] “This was at a time when we were just starting to test, and what we got into was failure after failure. We would fire the motor maybe a second and a half, and it would explode.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 261–263 (pre-Challenger)
- [SMI025] “It was things like turbine blades and sheet metal failures, and all of these things one after the other we kept encountering as we learned to get enough testing and design changes to get a full- duration test. We kept learning from testing.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 320–326 (pre-Challenger)
- [WHI039] “We went anywhere we had a weak tile and we replaced them with a stronger tile. We were constantly learning that through the program. When we found something out, we’d go check the other vehicles, and we do it not only with the tile; we do it with anything else. If we have an electrical issue with one, then we go look at all of the others in the same scenarios.” — White, `whitetr-7-12-11.txt` l. 741–749 (between accidents)
- [SHE083] “We spent six months of inspection and repair in the wiring systems, the however many hundreds of miles of wire we have on the vehicle, to make sure that we didn’t have any similar damage that could cause real problems.” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 2075–2079 (between accidents)

**Where the evidence is thin.** Mostly pre-Challenger development and early flights; informants describe their successes more readily than failures to learn.

### P2. Organizational lines divert concerns

**Proposition.** A concern whose cause sits in one element or organization and whose effect falls in another moves slowly, is disowned, or is deferred to the other side; it tends to end in negotiation over requirements or in accommodation rather than in evidence.

**Links.** T03 Concerns at organizational lines → T09 Flying with problems not fully resolved.

**Evidence.** 10 passages from 4 informants (Sheehan 6, Smith 2, Pessin 1, Mitchell 1); 10 first-hand; eras: pre-Challenger 6, between accidents 2, general/undated 1, Challenger/return to flight 1.

- [SHE003] “So we knew we had—at least we at Rockwell knew we had a problem that we needed to get the Program to recognize and define a requirement that the Tank preclude icing.” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 325–331 (pre-Challenger)
- [SHE005] “They weren’t interested in volunteering a couple thousand pounds of insulation to help those other [Orbiter] guys. They wanted to be directed that that is a Program requirement. Then they would be able to increase their weight bogey and not have to take the weight for [anti-icing] insulation out of the weight that they were allocated for structure and other Tank systems.” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 347–355 (pre-Challenger)
- [SHE006] “So it took about—oh, it was at least six months or maybe a year before we had briefed the Program with enough data that they actually recognized that there was a necessity to recognize an anti-icing requirement, I guess is the best way to say it.” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 357–361 (pre-Challenger)
- [SHE009] “I guess it was still a Program Requirements Control Board at the time, a PRCB, that baselined I think it was about 1,300 pounds of additional foam insulation on the Tank to preclude icing” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 445–453 (pre-Challenger)
- [SHE013] “they [had] a “don’t touch me” kind of attitude. Almost as bad as the Tank guys were, “Well, I don’t have a requirement to preclude ice.” So everybody was very, very parochial.” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 547–555 (pre-Challenger)
- [SMI151] “And there was always finger pointing, “It’s coming off the booster; it’s coming off the external tank.”” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 1806–1808 (between accidents)
- [SMI152] “We were convinced it wasn’t coming off the booster, and the tank people felt that “It’s not our insulation.” We were always going through that and continued to assess ways we could mitigate any debris coming off the motor. It was a major focus area.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 1810–1814 (between accidents)
- [PES040] “Really Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and to a degree Johnson, because when we dealt with the Johnson guys foam coming off was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter. It was never flight safety.” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 1437–1441 (general/undated)
- [SHE046] “I remember a lot of times where you’d hear, “We’ll let the Cape guys worry about that,” whether it was a test requirement or how to interface with a piece of hardware to do a checkout. That wasn’t their priority as designers.” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 1344–1352 (pre-Challenger)
- [MIT109] “The damage to that tile was blamed [by some] on that piece of cork, which Thiokol refuted, which we looked at and didn’t believe, and which other elements like the E tank [external tank] and the booster—booster elements are different than motor elements—[could have contributed]. The [booster] nose cone and the parachute compartment and all that is up ahead of us. That was a potential source for the impacts, [plus] the external tank. They had always shed some insulation and had caused little nicks in the orbiter so it was a big debate whether our piece of cork had caused the problem or not.” — Mitchell, `mitchellre-6-30-10.txt` l. 1969–1981 (Challenger/return to flight)

**Counter-evidence.**

- [SHE017] “So that confirmed that yes, there was a real issue with allowing “theoretically forming” ice to occur on the Tank, because it would in fact damage the tile.” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 602–606 (pre-Challenger)

**Where the evidence is thin.** The clearest case (External Tank icing) is Sheehan's alone. The debris boundary rests on Smith and Mitchell. The link from boundary to accommodation is an inference across informants, and in the icing case evidence (an improvised test, SHE017) did help settle the dispute.

### P3. Drift loop (tentative)

**Status: tentative.** Hindsight-based: told after the accidents about the two problems that caused them, and six of seven supporting passages are not first-hand.

**Proposition.** Accommodating a known problem — treating it as maintenance, explaining it away as harmless, or reasoning that it is covered by a second seal — keeps it in service and moves it out of view as a flight-safety issue.

**Links.** T09 Flying with problems not fully resolved → T02 Problems that stay out of sight.

**Evidence.** 7 passages from 3 informants (Pessin 4, Mitchell 2, Smith 1); 1 first-hand; eras: pre-Challenger 3, between accidents 3, general/undated 1.

- [PES040] “Really Marshall engineering, Martin engineering, and to a degree Johnson, because when we dealt with the Johnson guys foam coming off was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter. It was never flight safety.” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 1437–1441 (general/undated)
- [PES047] “The decisions were made, and the reasons were that the passive system was much easier, not just for ET but for the whole stack, the whole program. The issue of foam on the protuberances has always been a challenge. We felt that there were certain areas where you just couldn’t perfectly seal it, and we would get some small ice issues. The program basically was accepting those. Since then they’ve come back, done redesigns, and fixed those. But the whole issue of foam and orbiter tiles has always been a challenge.” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 1505–1515 (pre-Challenger; first-hand: unclear)
- [MIT045] “The case-to-nozzle joint had exhibited more postflight damage than the field joints prior to Challenger. There were a number of instances of O-ring damage both in the field joints and the case-to-nozzle joint, but the case- to-nozzle joint had more. The reason it was less of a concern was that the case-to-nozzle joint had two types of seals using O-rings.” — Mitchell, `mitchellre-6-30-10.txt` l. 955–963 (pre-Challenger; first-hand: no)
- [MIT051] “We found after flight, before Challenger, that sometimes that outer boot ring made of phenolic that held one end of this protective curtain would be broken. It was fairly well known that the break of that outer boot ring happened after motor burnout.” — Mitchell, `mitchellre-6-30-10.txt` l. 1059–1063 (pre-Challenger; first-hand: no)
- [SMI150] “The program had always been getting tile damage. Based on complex flow analyses the ET [external tank] Project, had rationalized that nothing big enough to really cause a problem will come off.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 1802–1806 (between accidents; first-hand: no)
- [PES041] “Two flights before Columbia, we lost a big chunk of foam. The ET project manager sent his deputy to the Program Requirements Change Board, Level II—Neil [E.] Otte was his deputy—to open an IFA, in-flight anomaly. The program said, “We don’t need an in-flight anomaly, we know about foam coming off.” The program manager turned to the ET project manager and said, “Do a study to see what you can do to improve it.”” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 1443–1451 (between accidents; first-hand: no)
- [PES044] “risk, we treated it as a routine engineering change, not as a “stop the world we got to get off,” not as a “ground the fleet” type of change. And that change was in work at the time of Columbia.” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 1473–1475 (between accidents; first-hand: no)

**Counter-evidence.**

- [WHI063] “They expected them to be severely eroded when it came back, and it was not. Then our repair criteria changed from thinking we could only do a couple of small repairs on the tile and it” — White, `whitetr-7-12-11.txt` l. 1241–1243 (pre-Challenger)
- [WHI064] “After that, they realized it wasn’t going to, then they changed our repair criteria, which meant we fixed a lot more tile than we took off. So an act of God actually helped us.” — White, `whitetr-7-12-11.txt` l. 1253–1255 (pre-Challenger)

**Where the evidence is thin.** Told in hindsight about the two problems that later caused accidents (O-ring erosion, foam), which invites hindsight bias. Six of seven supporting passages are not first-hand: Mitchell's two pre-Challenger accounts, Pessin's account of the early ice-protection decision (first-hand unclear), and Pessin's and Smith's accounts of the External Tank project after Pessin retired. Two passages (MIT051, PES047) support only that the problem stayed in service, not that it dropped out of view. White's account of a good flight loosening repair criteria (WHI063, WHI064) is kept as counter-evidence: the mechanism is the same, but White presents it as sound learning and no later harm is linked to it.

### P4. Pressure pushes closure ahead of evidence

**Proposition.** Schedule and budget pressure push teams to commit hardware before test results, remove contingency, and cut the instrumentation and tracking that would have made problems visible.

**Links.** T11 Schedule, money and the program's end → T06 Settling by evidence and outside expertise; T09 Flying with problems not fully resolved; T02 Problems that stay out of sight.

**Evidence.** 9 passages from 4 informants (Smith 5, Mitchell 2, Pessin 1, Singer 1); 9 first-hand; eras: Challenger/return to flight 5, pre-Challenger 3, after return to flight 1.

- [MIT079] “Of course a lot of the schedule compression had to do with risk. “We assume this test is going to be right, and we’re proceeding on getting ready for the next test with the same hardware.” It bit us with the outer boot ring redesign that never should have happened. We had to back up and backtrack.” — Mitchell, `mitchellre-6-30-10.txt` l. 1532–1538 (Challenger/return to flight)
- [MIT080] “Most of the time it became a matter of we’re willing to take the risk to go ahead and commit to the next test article, to the flight article, assuming that this test is going to be successful. Most of the time we were successful so we were able to turn around and bring on the new hardware and test it.” — Mitchell, `mitchellre-6-30-10.txt` l. 1538–1544 (Challenger/return to flight)
- [SMI111] “On the SRM Project, we were doing things in parallel. We were building development motors and flight motors at the same time. Normally it’s sequential. You design the hardware, you build the development hardware, you test it, you qualify it, then you build the flight motors. Well, we were doing both concurrently, taking a huge risk that the design wouldn’t change to the point that we would have to scrap all these motors we’re building for flight.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 1518–1526 (Challenger/return to flight)
- [SMI167] “The magnitude of the task was a major challenge—seven days a week, three shifts a day—it was just an incredible pace. Every time I’d show J.R. a schedule, he’d say, “You’ve got a little contingency here, take it out.”” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 1940–1944 (Challenger/return to flight)
- [SMI168] “I said, “I’ve got to have some contingency, J.R., or I will never be able to do the schedule.” He said, “I know it, but we’re going to do seven days a week, three shifts a day because we’ll get there faster that way. If I give you contingency you’ll use it all up.” That was his philosophy.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 1946–1954 (Challenger/return to flight)
- [SMI016] “This was when we realized an earlier decision had created a major problem in the development program. In an attempt to save money an engine was cancelled from the budget, and that engine was to be very highly instrumented” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 263–271 (pre-Challenger)
- [SMI017] “The decision to not build the motor drove us to a flight configuration where there are almost no pressure taps, no temperature sensors, none of the information that you need to know what’s happening inside the motor.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 271–277 (pre-Challenger)
- [PES073] “There was a tracking ship in the Indian Ocean to look for pieces, but it was a Navy ship and they were charging by the day. The program kept slipping so Level II canceled the tracking ship. We have never had any hard data as to what actually hits the water” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 2012–2018 (pre-Challenger)
- [SIN040] “For other changes, we had to consider if we could implement them during the life of the Shuttle. As I talked about before, even when you have a change certified, it may take two to three years before it can be implemented into the hardware production line, which means you couldn’t even get the change incorporated until the end of the program. That’s where we had to make some critical decisions on where are we safe today to continue flying with tender loving care [extra inspections, for example], versus where do we need to make a change.” — Singer, `singerja-7-21-10.txt` l. 812–822 (after return to flight)

**Counter-evidence.**

- [MIT053] “Well, it didn’t work. And we had already built flight motors with the involute design, and we sent them to the Cape [Canaveral, Florida] before we had that test to prove that the involute didn’t work. As a contingency, we had [also] built the old style, and we were able to swap out the motors without any program impact. But I wish we’d never tried the involute system, and I’m still mad at some people.” — Mitchell, `mitchellre-6-30-10.txt` l. 1106–1114 (Challenger/return to flight)

**Where the evidence is thin.** Concentrated in the post-Challenger redesign (Mitchell, Smith) and main-engine development (Smith). Contingency hardware sometimes absorbed the cost (MIT053).

### P5. Depth and proximity speed concerns toward closure

**Proposition.** Government engineers deep enough to challenge contractors, and experts placed next to the hardware and each other, let problems be raised and settled faster; when experts rotate away, rapport and speed are lost.

**Links.** T05 Technical depth and proximity that let concerns travel → T03 Concerns at organizational lines; T06 Settling by evidence and outside expertise.

**Evidence.** 10 passages from 5 informants (Smith 5, Pessin 2, Sheehan 1, Mitchell 1, White 1); 10 first-hand; eras: pre-Challenger 5, Challenger/return to flight 3, between accidents 1, general/undated 1.

- [PES001] “At Marshall, we typically had guys who were as strong or stronger than the contractor. I know the contractors were quite shocked when we would get started. We would go into a meeting and they would start, let’s say, in stress analysis. Marshall would show up with a dozen PhDs in stress analysis.” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 554–564 (pre-Challenger)
- [PES004] “We had Marshall manufacturing experts, Marshall materials experts, Marshall structural analysis experts sitting in these meetings, and they were free meetings for the people to ask questions. It wasn’t the kind of meeting where you sit back and you just listen. We encouraged our people to ask questions, and after the first couple of meetings the contractors knew what to expect.” — Pessin, `pessinma-6-30-10.txt` l. 688–698 (pre-Challenger)
- [SMI041] “NASA did individual post-test analysis, and Rocketdyne did theirs. After every test we looked at all the data, we compared notes to assess any and all anomalies that might have occurred.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 439–443 (pre-Challenger)
- [SMI042] “We built a competency on the NASA side, where we were technically capable of challenging the contractor. People like Otto [K.] Goetz and even J.R. were very competent people and helped to ensure that we were doing the best job possible.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 443–449 (pre-Challenger)
- [SHE084] “The expert in wiring installations came here so he would be able to address the problems real-time on the floor. “Eyes-on” kind of thing. It doesn’t do any good to have a fantastic expert 2,500 miles away when the problem comes up at 3:00 a.m. Sunday morning on the floor of the OPF. That guy 2,500 miles away is of questionable use, no matter how smart he is.” — Sheehan, `sheehangd-7-12-11.txt` l. 2081–2091 (between accidents)
- [SMI165] “I lobbied for a long time and finally got the head of Quality on the SRB Project as a part of my team co-located in the project office because I wanted him there. - [SMI166] “able to change the organization, get him on my team and it worked great, improved the communication flow. That was a major change and a significant help to me in trying to run the program.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 1934–1938 (Challenger/return to flight)
- [SMI193] “I always felt that it was the better management configuration, where you’re co-located together so that that there’s no reason to say, “You’re not communicating,” versus being located in different buildings.” — Smith, `smithgw-5-12-11.txt` l. 2276–2282 (general/undated)

Those held the full texts of Edmondson, Starbuck & Milliken, Vaughan (1997) and CAIB chapter 8. If you want them read, you could supply the PDFs or allow those hosts.

## What the comparison shows

- **Strongest agreement: the CAIB report.** Four of its organizational causes match our themes almost word for word:
  - "Reliance on past success" matches the drift loop (P3).
  - "Lack of integrated management across program elements" matches Sheehan's "very very very little integration of requirements between projects."
  - "Operational rather than developmental" matches Smith's "People kept declaring we're operational."
  - "Stifled professional differences of opinion" matches T04.

  **Caution:** the interviews were done in 2010–11, after the CAIB report had shaped NASA's vocabulary. Some of the agreement may be informants retelling the official account.
- **Vaughan:** the drift loop resembles normalization of deviance. Mitchell's "less of a concern" because of a second seal mirrors the review's "a second o-ring would back up the first." Where we differ: our data include accommodation that never led to harm (White), while Vaughan's case was chosen because of its outcome. Neither her study nor ours has a Thiokol voice.
- **Voice literature:**
  - **Agreement:** our finding that individual judgment reaches decisions when solicited (P6) fits Edmondson's and Detert & Burris's emphasis on leaders.
  - **Two differences:** most of our concerns cross organizational lines (contractor, element, launch site), which a team-level construct like psychological safety doesn't capture; and oral histories can't really show silence.
- **Learning after failure:**
  - **Dillon & Tinsley:** their near-miss mechanism (successes lowering perceived risk) explains the drift loop. Their distinction between near-misses and genuine successes may explain White's counter-case.
  - **Christianson et al.:** fits the accident dimension (restructuring, relating, reinterpreting). Our tentative P11 adds a limit: the learning stayed close to the failed element.
- **Method:** we follow Gioia's sequence, including holding back the literature until now. The main departure is that archival oral histories can't be re-asked. The paper must say so, and should present our scripted checks as a rigor device, not the "template" Gioia warns against.

**Two possible contributions are flagged in the notes, not yet claimable:** accommodation that does and doesn't turn into drift, and the post-Challenger flood of formal concerns that clogged closure. Neither should be claimed as new until the full texts, and Madsen & Desai at least, have been read.

I also checked the notes against the data. All 30 passages cited in them exist, and the quoted phrases match their passages. That check caught two errors of mine, now fixed: a mistyped proposition number ("P20" for C20), and one quote attributed to the second half of a passage that splits across a page break.

## 2. Normalization of deviance and the Challenger and Columbia literature

### Vaughan, D. (1996). *The Challenger launch decision.* University of Chicago Press.

**What it says (from the publisher description and Meiksins's review).** The
launch decision was "not skullduggery or misconduct but a disastrous mistake";
NASA insiders, "when repeatedly faced with evidence that something was wrong,
normalized the deviance so that it became acceptable to them" (publisher).
Meiksins (1997, p. 515) summarizes the argument: engineers and managers
"evaluated the evidence of o-ring damage using consensual procedures",
concluding the O-rings were "safe" because "a second o-ring would back up the
first"; a production-pressured culture accommodated compromise; "structural
secrecy" made it hard for administrators to "know" there was a problem; and the
"amoral calculation" account "makes little sense".

**Where our findings agree.**
- **The drift loop (P3, tentative)** is close to normalization of deviance:
  known anomalies treated as maintenance or explained away. The closest match
  is Mitchell's account of pre-Challenger O-ring damage being "less of a
  concern" because the joint "had two types of seals" (MIT045), which is
  Meiksins's "second o-ring would back up the first" almost exactly — but it
  is second-hand.
- **Schedule and budget pressure (T11, P4)** corresponds to the "culture of
  production".
- **Problems out of sight (T02) and concerns at organizational lines (T03, P2)**
  correspond to "structural secrecy".

**Where they differ or add.**
- **Not every accommodation is drift.** White's account of a good flight
  loosening repair criteria (WHI063, WHI064) has the same mechanism but no
  later harm, and he presents it as learning. Our data separate accommodation
  that later proved dangerous (foam, O-rings) from accommodation that did not.
  Vaughan's case is selected on the outcome; ours includes non-outcomes.
- **Scope.** Vaughan analyzes the launch decision and the history behind it.
  Our informants say almost nothing about the eve-of-launch teleconference
  (only Smith's second-hand remark that candidates were "implicated", SMI200–SMI201)
  and much more about day-to-day handling across 1972–2011 and both accidents.
- **A shared limitation.** Meiksins (p. 516) notes Vaughan's "relatively
  limited access to events at Morton Thiokol". Our sample has no Thiokol
  informant either; the contractor appears only through NASA and Rockwell eyes.

**Caution.** Because we have not read the book, the paper should cite Vaughan
for the concept and its publisher-level summary, and Meiksins for the details
above, not the book's specific arguments.

### Meiksins, P. (1997). Review of Vaughan. *Sociological Inquiry*, 67(4), 514–516.

Read in full. Used above. Also notes Vaughan "may read more into this than is
warranted" in denying misconduct (p. 515), and suggests interorganizational
hierarchy (NASA's reaction to a contractor's no-launch recommendation) shaped
voice (p. 516) — which our T03 and C24 (customer and contractor) speak to.

### Vaughan, D. (1990). Autonomy, interdependence, and social control: NASA and the space shuttle Challenger. *ASQ*, 35(2), 225–257.

**What it says (abstract via ERIC).** NASA's safety regulators failed to catch
flaws in management procedures and technical design; their effectiveness was
"inhibited by the autonomy and interdependence" of NASA and its regulators.

**Comparison.** After Challenger, an independent safety organization was
created (C26: "an independent voice that could holler 'Stop'", MIT029). Smith's
account adds what independence was like in practice: Quality staff "sitting
down in another building critiquing what we're doing, and all I got was
notes" (SMI163), until he co-located the head of Quality in his project office
and it "improved the communication flow" (SMI165, SMI166). This is a
first-hand view of the tension Vaughan's abstract names — independence versus
the information that comes from being close — after her period of study.

### Vaughan, D. (1997). The trickle-down effect. *California Management Review*, 39(2), 80–102.

**What it says (store and indexing summaries only).** Traces links between top
policy decisions and the choices of engineers and managers doing risky work;
the cause lay in organizational and environmental conditions before the
launch decision. **Comparison:** consistent with P4 (pressure shaping closure)
and with informants' own causal accounts (e.g. SHE045 on the turnaround
timeline "required" for the Agency's cost case to Congress). Not used beyond
this, since only summaries were read.

### Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003). *Report, Volume I.*

**What it says (Executive Summary, read in full).** Organizational causes
include "reliance on past success as a substitute for sound engineering
practices", "organizational barriers that prevented effective communication of
critical safety information and stifled professional differences of opinion",
"lack of integrated management across program elements", and
"mischaracterization of the Shuttle as operational rather than developmental".

**Where our findings agree — closely.**
- "Reliance on past success" ↔ the drift loop (P3) and "we know about foam
  coming off" (PES041).
- "Lack of integrated management across program elements" ↔ Sheehan's "very
  very very little integration of requirements between projects" (SHE037) and
  the debris disputes across elements (SMI151, SMI152; T03, P2, P11).
- "Operational rather than developmental" ↔ Smith: "People kept declaring we're
  operational, but we were doing the same flight readiness reviews" (SMI083).
- "Stifled professional differences of opinion" ↔ T04 and P6, though our data
  show judgment reaching decisions when solicited rather than being stifled.

**Caution (method).** The interviews were conducted in 2010–2011, years after
the CAIB report entered NASA's vocabulary. Some agreement may be informants
retelling the official account rather than independent confirmation. The
paper should say so. Chapter 8, where the Board applied normalization of
deviance to Columbia, was not read.

### Starbuck, W. H., & Milliken, F. J. (1988). Challenger: Fine-tuning the odds until something breaks. *JMS*, 25(4), 319–340.

**What it says (abstract).** "Past successes and acclimatization alter
decision-makers' beliefs about probabilities of future success"; fine-tuning
results from engineers and managers "pursuing partially inconsistent goals
while trying to learn from their experiences", and "continues until a serious
failure occurs".

**Comparison.** Agrees with P3 and with the weight trades in C20 (scrubbing
"excess margin" to the 1.4 requirement, PES059, PES063 — fine-tuning in the
literal sense). White's counter-evidence (WHI063, WHI064) is fine-tuning that
did not end in failure, a reminder that the same process reads as learning or
drift depending on the outcome. The "differing responsibilities of engineers
and managers" matches T04 (Smith's "the S&E position is" vs. his own view,
SMI092).

### Mahler, J. G., with Casamayou, M. H. (2009). *Organizational learning at NASA.* Georgetown University Press.

**What it says (publisher description and contents).** The Columbia board
concluded NASA "failed to learn"; Mahler examines "what NASA did to address
problems revealed by Challenger and its uneven efforts to institutionalize its
own findings". Chapters cover structures for processing information,
contractor relations, political and budgetary pressures, and organizational
culture.

**Comparison.** "Uneven efforts to institutionalize" is consistent with our
tentative P11 (Challenger's reset stayed close to the failed element). Her
chapter topics map onto our T02/T03 (information and organizational lines),
C24 (contractor relations) and T11 (pressures) — independent support for the
structure's shape. Our contribution relative to Mahler is the practitioner's
view of daily concern handling. **Not read**; cite only for the description.

---

## 3. Voice and silence

### Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. *ASQ*, 44(2), 350–383.

**What it says (abstract).** Team psychological safety is "a shared belief held
by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking"; in
51 manufacturing teams it was associated with learning behavior, which
mediated its effect on performance; team structures "such as context support
and team leader coaching" and shared beliefs shape outcomes.

**Where our findings agree.** P6: individual judgment reached decisions mainly
when a senior person asked for it — Lindstrom's "I want to know what you
think" (SMI092) — consistent with leader behavior shaping whether people speak.

**Where they differ.**
- **Level and boundary.** Edmondson's construct is a team-level belief. Most of
  our concern handling crosses organizations — contractor and NASA, element
  and element, design and launch site (T03, P2, P11). Psychological safety
  inside a team says little about a concern that has to cross a contract or a
  Center.
- **Costs are personal, not interpersonal only.** Our C10 is about careers and
  standing ("my career will end here", SMI126; a boss "very upset", SMI093),
  closer to Milliken et al. (2003) than to team climate.
- **What oral histories can show.** Silence is an absence; retrospective
  interviews with people who stayed in the program are poorly placed to
  record it. We should not claim our data show low or high psychological
  safety.

**Correction carried from stage 1.** The project notes cited this work as
Edmondson (2001); it is 1999.

### Detert, J. R., & Burris, E. R. (2007). Leadership behavior and employee voice. *AMJ*, 50(4), 869–884.

**What it says (abstract).** In a restaurant chain (3,149 employees, 223
managers), managerial openness was the more consistent predictor of
improvement-oriented voice, and the relationship was mediated by perceived
psychological safety.

**Comparison.** Supports P6 directly. Our case adds that openness was often
exercised one level up, past the immediate boss (Lindstrom past Smith's chief
engineer, SMI092–SMI094), which created the "bind with your boss" Smith
describes (SMI095).

### Morrison, E. W., & Milliken, F. J. (2000). Organizational silence. *AMR*, 25(4), 706–725.

**What it says (abstract wording, as reproduced).** Silence as a
"collective-level phenomenon", with contextual conditions and collective
sensemaking producing "the shared perception that speaking up is unwise".

**Comparison.** Sheehan's "We all did 'wink-wink,' 'nod-nod,' 'yep sure,'
that's the timeline" (SHE045) is a collective going-along of the kind the
abstract describes — but it is one passage. Our data offer little else that
documents silence directly (see the caution under Edmondson).

### Milliken, F. J., Morrison, E. W., & Hewlin, P. F. (2003). An exploratory study of employee silence. *JMS*, 40(6), 1453–1476.

**What it says (abstract).** Most of 40 interviewees had stayed silent about a
concern; the most frequent reason was "fear of being viewed or labeled
negatively, and as a consequence, damaging valued relationships".

**Comparison.** C10 (personal exposure) agrees on the existence of personal
costs, but our informants describe speaking despite them, not staying silent.
This is a selection effect of who gets interviewed for a program history.

### Morrison, E. W. (2014). Employee voice and silence. *ARO*, 1, 173–197.

**What it says (abstract).** Defines upward voice — communicating
"suggestions, concerns, information about problems, or work-related opinions
to someone in a higher organizational position" — and reviews antecedents and
outcomes.

**Where our findings differ — and may add.**
- **Direction.** Much of our D2 is lateral and across organizations, not
  upward: contractor to program (SHE003), element to element (SMI151), launch
  site to designers (SHE046).
- **Institutionalized voice, and too much of it.** Formal channels turn voice
  into a procedure: a review item discrepancy is "in essence a concern that
  somebody has raised" (SMI135). After Challenger these channels were flooded
  — "six to seven thousand review item discrepancies" (SMI137), "quit writing
  these things, because it's killing us" (SMI142) — and pace had to be
  restored (P9). The voice literature, as summarized in these abstracts,
  centers on too little voice; our P9 documents a period of too much formal
  voice clogging closure. This is a candidate contribution, to be checked
  against the full texts before it is claimed.

---

## 4. Learning after failure

### Dillon, R. L., & Tinsley, C. H. (2008). How near-misses influence decision making under risk. *Management Science*, 54(8), 1425–1440.

**What it says (abstract).** Organizations learn from obvious failures but not
from near-misses, "events in which chance played a role in averting failure",
because such events are evaluated as successes and lower perceived risk.

**Comparison.** Gives P3 a mechanism: foam losses that did no serious harm were
"always a refurbish issue" (PES040) and the program declined an in-flight
anomaly because "we know about foam coming off" (PES041). It also sharpens our
counter-evidence: White's hail repair (WHI063, WHI064) may be a resilient
success rather than a near-miss; Dillon and Tinsley's distinction lets the
paper separate the two instead of treating all accommodation as drift.

### Christianson, M. K., Farkas, M. T., Sutcliffe, K. M., & Weick, K. E. (2009). Learning through rare events. *Organization Science*, 20(5), 846–860.

**What it says (abstract).** Rare events are interruptions that "expose
weaknesses and reveal unrealized behavioral potential"; organizations learn
"through" them as routines of interpreting, relating and re-structuring are
strengthened.

**Comparison.** D4 reads well in these terms: re-structuring after Challenger
(T12 outside eyes; independent safety), relating (T13, "We didn't point
fingers", MIT119; NASA moving into the contractor's plant, MIT003), and
re-interpreting after Columbia (T15, "I believe you, but demonstrate it",
SIN036). Our tentative P11 adds a limit: the learning that Challenger
triggered stayed close to the failed element.

### Madsen & Desai (2010); Cannon & Edmondson (2005)

Verified as existing works; **content not accessed** (no abstracts obtained).
Madsen and Desai study learning from failure and success in orbital launch
vehicles and are the most directly relevant quantitative study; Cannon and
Edmondson address barriers to learning from failure. Both should be read
before the Discussion is written; neither is used as evidence here.

---

## 5. Method: Gioia, Corley & Hamilton (2013)

Read in full. Where our procedure follows the method, and where it departs:

| Gioia et al. (2013) | Our study |
|:-|:-|
| 1st-order analysis "tries to adhere faithfully to informant terms" (p. 20) | Open codes and concept labels use informants' phrases; labels must be first-hand quotes (enforced by the build). |
| 2nd-order themes, then aggregate dimensions; data structure (pp. 20–21) | 37 concepts → 15 themes → 4 dimensions; blind checks at both levels. |
| "Semi-ignorance" of the literature until the data structure (p. 21) | Followed: the project notes' literature-derived dimensions were dropped in stage 1; literature first consulted here. |
| Informants as "knowledgeable agents"; "backtrack" to informants with new questions (pp. 17, 26) | **Departure.** Archival oral histories: NASA's interviewers asked the questions, and no informant can be re-asked. The paper must state this. |
| Grounded model makes relationships "transparent" (p. 22); data structure "does not account very well for chains of events" (note 4) | 14 propositions with passage-level evidence and a period table. |
| Propositions are optional (p. 25) | We include them, with status labels (supported, tentative, interpretation). |
| Warns against using the method as a "template" or "cookbook" (pp. 25–26) | A risk to name: our procedure is unusually codified (scripts, checks). The paper should present it as a rigor device, not a recipe. |

---

## 6. What could not be accessed

- **Full texts not read:** Vaughan (1996) book; Vaughan (1990); Vaughan (1997);
  CAIB Vol. I chapter 8; Edmondson (1999); Starbuck & Milliken (1988); Detert &
  Burris (2007); Morrison & Milliken (2000); Milliken et al. (2003); Morrison
  (2014); Dillon & Tinsley (2008); Christianson et al. (2009); Mahler (2009);
  Starbuck & Farjoun (2005) and its chapters.
- **No abstract at all:** Madsen & Desai (2010); Cannon & Edmondson (2005).
- **Blocked by permission during this project:** web.mit.edu,
  fenix.iseg.ulisboa.pt, govinfo.library.unt.edu, history.nasa.gov (stage 1);
  dash.harvard.edu, pages.stern.nyu.edu, www.iot.ntnu.no, s3.amazonaws.com
  (this stage). Not retried by other routes.
- **Returned 403:** the AOM page for Madsen & Desai; the University of Texas
  repository copy of Haunschild's (2009) review of Mahler.

**What this means for the paper.** Claims about Vaughan, Edmondson and the voice
literature should be limited to what their abstracts and the review state, or
the full texts should be obtained first. The two candidate contributions
flagged above — accommodation that does and does not become drift (§4,
Dillon & Tinsley), and post-accident excess of formal voice (§3, Morrison) —
should not be claimed as novel until the full texts, and at least Madsen &
Desai, are read.

# Raising and closing technical concerns in the Space Shuttle program: A recurring cycle, reset twice

## Abstract

How did engineers and managers in the Space Shuttle program raise and handle technical safety concerns, and how did the Challenger (1986) and Columbia (2003) accidents change those practices? We analyze seven oral histories recorded by NASA's STS Recordation Oral History Project in 2010–2011 with engineers, managers and a technician who worked on the solid rocket motor and booster, the External Tank, and the Orbiter's thermal protection system. Following Gioia, Corley and Hamilton (2013), we coded 768 passages into 37 first-order concepts, 15 second-order themes and four aggregate dimensions, and built a grounded model of 14 propositions. Informants describe a recurring cycle in which problems surface, must travel to someone who can act on them, and are closed either by fixing them or by flying with them. Organizational lines, schedule pressure, technical depth and proximity, and individual judgment speed or divert that cycle. Challenger reset it for the failed element, chiefly by changing who looks at a problem and who decides; tentatively, Columbia changed what counts as enough to fly. Several propositions rest on few informants or on second-hand accounts, and we mark them as tentative.

## 1. Introduction

The two Space Shuttle accidents are classic cases in organization studies of how organizations handle warning signs. Much is known about the launch decisions themselves. Less is known about how the engineers and managers who lived through the program describe raising, escalating and settling technical concerns day to day, and about what each accident changed in that work. Near the end of the program, NASA's STS Recordation Oral History Project interviewed many of these people, and the edited transcripts are public.

This paper asks: *How did engineers and managers in the Shuttle program raise and handle technical safety concerns, and how did the two accidents change those practices?* We answer it inductively, in the Gioia tradition (Gioia, Corley, & Hamilton, 2013), from seven oral histories covering four decades of the program — from design in the 1970s to the last flights in 2011.

Our contribution is a grounded model of concern handling as a recurring cycle. Problems surface through the hardware and through the people who handle, test and fly it, or they stay out of sight. A concern then has to travel — often across the line between NASA and a contractor, between one element of the vehicle and another, or between designers and the launch site — to someone who can act on it. It is closed in one of two ways: by fixing it, with evidence or by adding protection, or by continuing to fly with the problem not fully resolved. The first route feeds a learning loop; the second, tentatively, a drift loop in which a known problem drops out of view as a safety issue. Each accident reset this cycle in a different way. In the informants' accounts, Challenger changed who looks at a problem and who decides; tentatively, Columbia changed what counts as enough to fly.

We present the model with its limits. Seven informants cannot speak for the program; only 41 of our 768 passages describe the years between the accidents; and some of the most consequential links rest on one or two informants or on second-hand accounts. We label each proposition as supported, tentative, or our interpretation, and we report where the evidence is thin.

## 2. Background

**Normalization of deviance and the Challenger case.** Vaughan's (1996) study of the Challenger launch decision argues that it was "not skullduggery or misconduct but a disastrous mistake": NASA insiders, "when repeatedly faced with evidence that something was wrong, normalized the deviance so that it became acceptable to them" (publisher's description). In Meiksins's (1997) summary, engineers and managers judged the O-rings safe because "a second o-ring would back up the first", a production-pressured culture accommodated compromise, and "structural secrecy" made it hard for administrators to know there was a problem. Starbuck and Milliken (1988) describe a related process of fine-tuning: "Past successes and acclimatization alter decision-makers' beliefs about probabilities of future success", and fine-tuning "continues until a serious failure occurs". Vaughan (1990) argues that the effectiveness of NASA's safety regulators was inhibited by the autonomy and interdependence of NASA and its regulators.

**Columbia and organizational learning.** The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003) located the accident's organizational causes in the program's history and culture, including "reliance on past success as a substitute for sound engineering practices", "organizational barriers that prevented effective communication of critical safety information and stifled professional differences of opinion", "lack of integrated management across program elements", and the "mischaracterization of the Shuttle as operational rather than developmental". Mahler (2009) examines what NASA did after Challenger and its "uneven efforts to institutionalize its own findings".

**Voice and silence.** Upward voice is communicating "suggestions, concerns, information about problems, or work-related opinions to someone in a higher organizational position" (Morrison, 2014). Edmondson (1999) defines team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking" and links it to learning behavior. Detert and Burris (2007) find that managerial openness predicts employees' improvement-oriented voice, with psychological safety mediating the relationship. Morrison and Milliken (2000) treat silence as a "collective-level phenomenon", and Milliken, Morrison and Hewlin (2003) find that employees most often stay silent for "fear of being viewed or labeled negatively".

**Learning after failure.** Dillon and Tinsley (2008) argue that organizations learn from obvious failures but not from near-misses — "events in which chance played a role in averting failure" — because near-misses are evaluated as successes. Christianson, Farkas, Sutcliffe and Weick (2009) find that rare events are interruptions that "expose weaknesses and reveal unrealized behavioral potential".

As summarized here, these works center on decisions at or near the moment of failure, and on concerns moving up a hierarchy. Our informants instead describe day-to-day concern handling across four decades, much of it moving sideways across organizational lines. Following Gioia et al. (2013), we did not use these works to build our categories; we consulted them only after the data structure and model were complete.

## 3. Data and methods

### 3.1 Data

Our data are seven oral histories from NASA's STS Recordation Oral History Project, recorded in 2010 and 2011 by NASA historians (Table 1). From ten candidate interviews we chose seven that together cover both accidents and include engineers, managers and one technician; three were screened out because they said little about either accident or, in one case, belonged to a different NASA oral history project. The seven informants worked on the elements implicated in the two accidents — the solid rocket motor and booster (Challenger), and the External Tank and the Orbiter's thermal protection system (Columbia) — and on main engine development before Challenger.

{{TABLE1}}

The transcripts are edited records, not verbatim ones: each is headed "Edited Oral History Transcript" and contains bracketed editorial insertions. We quote the edited transcripts exactly, keeping the brackets. Six long bracketed blocks in Mitchell's transcript read as text he added when editing it rather than speech from the interview; passages inside them are kept in the analysis but never counted as first-hand evidence, and none is quoted in this paper.

### 3.2 Analysis

We followed Gioia et al. (2013). The unit of analysis is a *passage*: a contiguous stretch of the informant's own speech, usually one to six sentences, describing one instance or practice of noticing, raising, escalating, reviewing, deciding on, accepting, deferring or settling a technical problem, or a change in such a practice. Biography and purely technical description were not coded, nor were material about other programs (such as Apollo) or bare answers to an interviewer's yes-or-no question.

*Open coding.* Each transcript was coded in full, with labels kept close to the informant's words — what Gioia et al. call a first-order analysis that "tries to adhere faithfully to informant terms" — and with no literature terms used as codes. The open coding was carried out by AI coding agents (Anthropic's Claude), one per transcript, working to written rules with no target number of passages and no example phrases. Every stretch of speech a coder considered and left uncoded was logged with a reason (367 stretches). Every quotation was checked by script against the cited transcript lines. Each passage was also tagged with the period it describes and whether the informant had first-hand knowledge of it. A blind re-tagging of a stratified 10% sample (76 passages) disagreed on 12; on checking the transcripts, 5 were errors, which we corrected. We therefore estimate an error rate of 6.6% in the era and first-hand tags.

*From passages to concepts, themes and dimensions.* The 768 passages were grouped from their full quotations into 37 first-order concepts. Each passage has one primary concept, and 227 also have a secondary one. Each concept is labelled with a first-hand phrase taken from its own quotations. The concepts were then grouped into 15 second-order themes and four aggregate dimensions, which form the data structure (Figure 1). Concept and theme grouping was done by Claude in dialogue with the author, who reviewed and accepted, changed or rejected each decision.

*Blind checks.* Two separate AI analysts, given no access to our categories, regrouped the material independently. At the passage level, the blind grouping (66 groups) and ours share an adjusted Rand index of 0.28. Most of the difference is finer splitting: 64% of passages fall in a blind group that sits mainly inside one of our concepts. At the theme level, from concept labels and definitions alone, agreement was 0.56 for themes and 0.63 for dimensions, and seven of the fifteen themes were identical. We re-read the quotations behind each disagreement and revised the structure where they supported the blind analyst. The remaining disagreements and our reasons for keeping our grouping are recorded with the data structure.

*Grounded model.* We related the themes to one another and over time in 14 propositions (Table 3). Each proposition is tied to specific passages, and each passage must belong to one of the themes it links. We label each proposition *supported* (first-hand passages from three or more informants), *tentative* (fewer informants, mostly second-hand passages, or an inference across informants), or *our interpretation* (a claim no informant makes). Only after the model was complete did we consult the literature, as Gioia et al. recommend.

### 3.3 Departures from the method

Gioia et al. (2013) treat informants as knowledgeable agents to be re-interviewed — to "backtrack" — as the analysis develops. Our informants were interviewed by others, about the program as a whole, and cannot be re-asked; our questions are not the interviewers'. The interviews also took place years after the Columbia board's report entered NASA's vocabulary, so some agreement between informants and the report may reflect retelling rather than independent observation. Finally, our procedure is unusually codified — scripts check quotations, placements and labels. We use it as a check on rigor, not as the "template" or "cookbook" Gioia et al. warn against.

**D1. Surfacing problems.** Problems became visible through the hardware itself (T01). A technician at the External Tank contractor noticed a bad lot of material that had passed receiving checks: “This isn’t the same stuff I’ve been spraying.” (Pessin, l. 968–978). On the tile line, finding a defect meant tracing it: “We have to bound it, see how far it goes.” (White, l. 1121–1127). In main-engine development, “We kept learning from testing.” (Smith, l. 320–326). Other problems stayed out of sight (T02): suppliers changed materials unannounced — “we didn’t know the change had been made” (Pessin, l. 1089–1095); failure modes were not understood — “All of us didn’t understand the risk” (Pessin, l. 1406–1410); and after Challenger the redesign team found requirements met only on paper: “We had certified it by analysis.” (Smith, l. 1645–1649).

**D2. Moving concerns to where they can be acted on.** A concern that crossed an organizational line (T03) moved slowly, was disowned, or was pushed to the other side. Getting the program to own the External Tank icing problem took “at least six months or maybe a year before we had briefed the Program with enough data” (Sheehan, l. 357–361). Booster and tank projects each denied that debris was theirs; the tank people felt that “It’s not our insulation.” (Smith, l. 1810–1814). Designers deferred launch-site consequences: “We’ll let the Cape guys worry about that,” (Sheehan, l. 1344–1352). Within the line of authority (T04), informants describe “the honest technical interchanges” (Sheehan, l. 884–888), a senior manager asking past the official position — “I want to know what you think.” (Smith, l. 1148–1154) — and the personal stakes of owning a problem: “my career will end here” (Smith, l. 1627–1633). Technical depth and proximity let concerns travel (T05). At Marshall, “We encouraged our people to ask questions” (Pessin, l. 688–698). At the launch site, “It doesn’t do any good to have a fantastic expert 2,500 miles away when the problem comes up at 3:00 a.m. Sunday morning on the floor of the OPF.” (Sheehan, l. 2081–2091). The cost of distance shows in White's account of rotating engineers: “about time you build a good rapport with an engineer working your issues, then, bingo, he was back in California.” (White, l. 1443–1447).

**D3. Closing technical questions.** Informants describe several ways questions were closed. Evidence and outside expertise were the arbiter (T06): “testing always was the ultimate referee of how good our design was” (Mitchell, l. 708–712); after Challenger, “the team traced each leg of the fault tree” (Thomas, l. 179–183); and parallel teams brought “fresh eyeballs” (Mitchell, l. 443–445). Formal channels and decision rights closed questions (T07): “You have to deal with every one of them.” (Mitchell, l. 1872–1880), and “There was not necessarily always consensus, but we moved on as I had the final vote.” (Thomas, l. 416–422). Committing to fly carried weight (T08): “seven lives are riding on us being right” (Singer, l. 951–961).

Two routes to closure point in opposite directions. In the first, the program flew with problems not fully resolved (T09). It reclassified them: “foam coming off was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter. It was never flight safety.” (Pessin, l. 1437–1441). It decided on incomplete evidence: “We had a most-probable explanation” (Smith, l. 889–897), or “we did what we could do that night, and they flew” (White, l. 1235–1239). It contained them: “we had to pull the pump after each flight and examine them” (Smith, l. 395–397). And it traded margin for weight: “an acceptable issue to gain 800 pounds” (Pessin, l. 1789–1795). In the second route, the program added protection beyond what the evidence required (T10): “Because we could not put that problem to bed, we could not characterize the possibility of circumferential flow.” (Mitchell, l. 908–926); “I didn’t think it was necessary but we kept it as a redundant way” (Thomas, l. 596–600); or it designed against debris because “it could hit the Orbiter” (Smith, l. 164–168). Schedule, money and, late on, the program's end bore on both routes (T11): “It bit us with the outer boot ring redesign that never should have happened.” (Mitchell, l. 1532–1538); “we had to ask ourselves if we could even get a change incorporated before we flew out the assets” (Singer, l. 416–426).

**D4. Resetting after the accidents.** After Challenger, the commission's requirements and new oversight put outside eyes on the solid rocket motor redesign (T12): an “independent voice that could holler” stop (Mitchell, l. 629–631), and panels that were “extremely cooperative, but rigorous in their oversight” (Mitchell, l. 606–612) and “really challenged us” (Smith, l. 1585–1589). People and relations were reset (T13): new leaders who were “not on the project at the time of the accident” (Mitchell, l. 244–250), and an effort to end blame between NASA and the contractor — “We didn’t point fingers.” (Mitchell, l. 2316–2322). Caution over-corrected and was pulled back (T14): the processing team became “overzealous with the number of measurements and inspections” (Thomas, l. 1016–1024); a manager asked his Center Director to tell Engineering to “quit writing these things, because it’s killing us” (Smith, l. 1741–1743); and at the tile shop the commission's finding “that the shop folks had too much control” (White, l. 1650–1654) brought far more paperwork until the shop asked, “What are you doing with all this data?” (White, l. 2518–2524). After Columbia (T15), accepted explanations had to be demonstrated — “I believe you, but demonstrate it.” (Singer, l. 741–745) — and “after the Columbia incident, our criteria changed” (White, l. 924–930).

## 5. The grounded model

Figure 2 relates the themes to one another and over time; Table 3 lists the 14 propositions with their status and evidence. The model has three parts: a concern-handling cycle present in every period, four conditions that speed or divert it, and the changes each accident brought. Its claims about change over time are only as strong as the passages from each period: 290 describe the years before Challenger, 261 the Challenger investigation and return to flight, 41 the years between the accidents, 46 the Columbia investigation and return to flight, 23 the last years of flight, and 107 are undated.
