### 5.1 The cycle and its two loops

*Learning loop (P1, supported).* Problems that surface in the hardware are usually chased to a cause and fixed, and the fix is carried across the fleet. When the soft heat sink was found, the materials engineers traced it to the tile waterproofing (White, l. 1127–1131); a weak tile found on one orbiter led the shop to check the other vehicles (White, l. 741–749); and an in-flight wiring short led to six months of inspection across the fleet (Sheehan, l. 2075–2079).

*Drift loop (P3, tentative).* Accommodating a known problem — treating it as maintenance, explaining it away, or reasoning that a second seal covers it — keeps it in service and moves it out of view as a flight-safety issue. Pessin says of foam loss that “It was never flight safety.” (Pessin, l. 1437–1441). His account of the year before Columbia — the program declining to open an in-flight anomaly after a large foam loss, and the fix proceeding as a routine change still in work when Columbia was lost (Pessin, l. 1443–1451; l. 1473–1475) — is second-hand, as he had retired. So is Smith's report that the tank project reasoned that nothing large enough to cause a problem would come off (Smith, l. 1802–1806), and Mitchell's account of pre-Challenger O-ring damage judged less of a concern because of a second seal (Mitchell, l. 955–963). We hold P3 as tentative because six of its seven supporting passages are not first-hand and all are told in hindsight about the two problems that later caused accidents. White's account of a flight that came back in better shape than feared, after which repair criteria were relaxed (White, l. 1241–1243; l. 1253–1255), is counter-evidence: the same mechanism, presented as sound learning, with no later harm.

### 5.2 Four conditions

*Organizational lines divert concerns (P2, supported).* A concern whose cause sits in one element or organization and whose effect falls in another moves slowly, is disowned, or is deferred, and tends to end in negotiation over requirements or in accommodation rather than in evidence. The tank's designers would not add insulation for the Orbiter's sake unless directed to (Sheehan, l. 347–355); booster and tank projects pointed at each other over debris (Smith, l. 1806–1808). In the icing case, an improvised test did help settle the dispute, so evidence is not always absent.

*Pressure pushes closure ahead of evidence (P4, supported).* Schedule and budget pressure led teams to commit hardware before test results (Mitchell, l. 1538–1544; Smith, l. 1518–1526) and cut instrumentation and tracking that would have made problems visible (Smith, l. 263–277; Pessin, l. 2012–2018).

*Depth and proximity speed concerns toward closure (P5, supported).* Engineers able to challenge contractors, and experts placed near the hardware and each other, let problems be raised and settled faster; Smith found that co-locating the head of Quality with his project improved communication (Smith, l. 1934–1938). These claims come mostly from the people who built the arrangements.

*Individual judgment reaches the decision when asked for (P6, supported).* A person's own technical judgment changed a decision mainly when a senior person asked for it or when the person held data the decision-maker lacked — Sheehan's check of actual flight loads (Sheehan, l. 1643–1655), White's request to rerun a cure test (White, l. 2020–2024) — and stating it against one's own organization was costly: Smith's boss was upset with him (Smith, l. 1156). Smith supplies half the evidence, and in one case engineering's view prevailed over his as project manager (Smith, l. 1635–1639).

### 5.3 What Challenger changed

After Challenger, the commission's requirements and outside reviewers pushed closure in the redesigned motor toward full-scale test evidence and toward protection beyond what the team's own tests required — joint heaters that Thomas judged unnecessary on his team's test evidence were added at the oversight panel's insistence (Thomas, l. 782–786; P7, supported). Leaders new to the project were brought in, NASA moved its team into the contractor's plant, and NASA managers worked to stop the mutual blame (Mitchell, l. 283–293; Smith, l. 1897–1903; P8, supported), though Smith describes a strained relationship with the contractor's program manager throughout. The swing to caution flooded the formal channels — thousands of review item discrepancies months before flight (Smith, l. 1706–1712), repair records growing from three pages to twenty-one (White, l. 2497–2501) — until managers restored pace with decision authority (Thomas, l. 1024–1030) and the tile shop won back standard repairs (White, l. 2550–2554; P9, supported). For those who flew the redesigned hardware, committing to fly felt heavier and stayed so (Smith, l. 2168–2176; P10, supported).

Tentatively (P11), Challenger's reset stayed close to the failed element. Elements not implicated changed little: for the External Tank, a stricter rule that all cracks go to engineering review (Pessin, l. 2429–2441); for the tiles, more documentation (White, l. 2493–2497). Between the accidents, debris crossing element lines was still argued over and accommodated (Smith, l. 1800–1808). The link between the two halves of this proposition is our inference, the between-accident evidence is thin, and the passages on the path to Columbia are second-hand.

### 5.4 What Columbia and the program's end changed

Tentatively (P12), Columbia changed the standard of proof. Engineers gained more latitude to question inherited explanations (Singer, l. 668–670), risk was presented in more detail (Singer, l. 745–753), repair criteria tightened, and in-flight imaging made damage visible (White, l. 2094–2098). This rests on two informants: Singer for the standard of proof, White for criteria and imaging. No informant was a decision-maker for the External Tank or the program at the time of Columbia. Also tentatively (P13), in the last years the time a change took to reach the hardware pushed decisions toward continued flight with extra inspection rather than hardware change, with changes reserved for safety (Singer, l. 812–826); this rests almost entirely on Singer.

### 5.5 A contrast, offered as our interpretation

Read together, P7–P12 suggest that Challenger mainly changed *who looks at a problem and who decides* — an independent safety organization, outside panels, control moved from the shop to engineering — while Columbia mainly changed *what counts as enough to fly*: demonstration and stricter criteria (P14). No informant states this contrast. White is the only informant with first-hand accounts of both resets.

## 6. Discussion

**Drift, and accommodation that is not drift.** The drift loop (P3) resembles Vaughan's (1996) normalization of deviance as summarized by her publisher and by Meiksins (1997): anomalies redefined as acceptable, and redundancy — a second seal — taken as reassurance. It also resembles the Columbia board's "reliance on past success as a substitute for sound engineering practices" (CAIB, 2003). Our data add a distinction. Accommodation that later proved dangerous (foam, O-rings) sits beside accommodation that did not: White's relaxed repair criteria after a flight that went better than feared. Dillon and Tinsley's (2008) distinction between near-misses, where chance averted failure, and other successes offers a way to tell the two apart. The question is not whether a problem was lived with, but whether the evidence that it was tolerable came from chance. Because P3 is tentative and told in hindsight, we offer this as a direction for research rather than a finding.

**Voice across organizational lines.** The voice literature summarized above concerns communication to "someone in a higher organizational position" (Morrison, 2014), and psychological safety is defined at the level of the team (Edmondson, 1999). Much of the concern handling our informants describe moves sideways: from contractor to program, between elements, and between designers and the launch site (T03, P2). Our finding that individual judgment reached decisions mainly when senior people asked for it (P6) fits Detert and Burris's (2007) finding that managerial openness predicts voice. But boundaries between organizations, which a team-level construct does not capture, are where our informants place most delays and disputes. The data also show voice built into procedure — review item discrepancies, material review boards, launch-day polling (T07) — and, after Challenger, that formal voice multiplying until it clogged closure (P9). The works summarized here focus on too little voice. Whether formal voice multiplying after a failure is a recognized phenomenon in the fuller literature should be checked before it is claimed as a contribution.

**Learning through rare events, and its reach.** Christianson et al. (2009) describe rare events as interruptions that "expose weaknesses and reveal unrealized behavioral potential". Our accident dimension fits that description: re-structuring after Challenger (outside eyes, independent safety), relating (new leaders, and an effort to build “one team” (Smith, l. 1867–1871)), and re-interpreting after Columbia (demonstration). Our tentative P11 adds a limit: the learning Challenger set off stayed close to the element that failed. This is consistent with Mahler's (2009) account of NASA's "uneven efforts to institutionalize its own findings", and with the Columbia board's finding of a "lack of integrated management across program elements" (CAIB, 2003).

**Transferable concepts.** Gioia et al. (2013) ask inductive studies to extract concepts that travel. We offer three. First, concern handling as a cycle with two loops, learning and drift, whose balance depends on how questions are closed. Second, organizational lines as a condition that diverts concerns from evidence to negotiation. Third — as our interpretation — failures may reset different parts of the cycle: who looks and decides, or what counts as enough.

## 7. Limitations

*Sample.* Seven informants cannot speak for the program. There is no informant from Thiokol, the solid rocket motor contractor, and none who decided for the External Tank or the program at the time of Columbia. One informant (White) is a technician and supervisor rather than an engineer or manager. Sheehan worked for a contractor throughout.

*Data.* The oral histories were recorded by others, years after both accidents, and could not be followed up. Informants may retell the Columbia board's account rather than report independently. The transcripts are edited, and passages that Mitchell appears to have added when editing are excluded from first-hand evidence. Only 41 of 768 passages describe the years between the accidents, which limits what we can say about Challenger's lasting effects and the path to Columbia.

*Evidence for the model.* P3, P11, P12 and P13 are tentative. P3 rests largely on second-hand, hindsight accounts, as do the passages on the path to Columbia in P11. P12 and P13 rest on one or two informants. P14 is our interpretation, not a claim any informant makes. Four concepts rest on a single informant: C09 (Smith), C20 (Pessin), C26 (Mitchell) and C32 (Singer).

*Coding.* A blind audit estimates a 6.6% error rate in the era and first-hand tags. Open coding was done by AI coding agents, and grouping by an AI analyst under the author's review. Independent blind regroupings agreed only partly with ours (adjusted Rand index 0.28 for passages; 0.56 for themes and 0.63 for dimensions).

*Literature.* We did not read the full texts of Vaughan (1996) or Edmondson (1999). Our claims about them rest on the publisher's description, the published abstract and Meiksins's (1997) review. The other works are cited only for what their abstracts state, and the CAIB report for its Executive Summary. Works we could verify only by their bibliographic details are not cited.

# Raising and closing technical concerns in the Space Shuttle program: A recurring cycle, reset twice

## Abstract

How did engineers and managers in the Space Shuttle program raise and handle technical safety concerns, and how did the Challenger (1986) and Columbia (2003) accidents change those practices? We analyze seven oral histories recorded by NASA in 2010–2011 with engineers, managers and a technician. Following Gioia, Corley and Hamilton (2013), we coded 768 passages into 37 concepts, 15 themes and four dimensions, and built a grounded model of 14 propositions. Informants describe a recurring cycle: problems surface, must travel to someone who can act on them, and are closed either by fixing them or by flying with them. Organizational lines, schedule pressure, technical depth and proximity, and individual judgment speed or divert that cycle. Challenger reset it for the failed element, chiefly by changing who looks at a problem and who decides; tentatively, Columbia changed what counts as enough to fly. Several propositions rest on few informants or second-hand accounts, and we mark them as tentative.

## 1. Introduction

The Shuttle accidents are classic cases of how organizations handle warning signs. Much is known about the launch decisions; less about how the people who lived through the program describe raising and settling technical concerns day to day, and what each accident changed in that work. NASA's STS Recordation Oral History Project interviewed many of them near the end of the program.

We ask: *How did engineers and managers in the Shuttle program raise and handle technical safety concerns, and how did the two accidents change those practices?* We answer inductively, following Gioia et al. (2013), from seven oral histories spanning design in the 1970s to the last flights in 2011.

Our model treats concern handling as a recurring cycle. Problems surface through the hardware or stay out of sight; a concern travels — often across the line between NASA and a contractor, between elements of the vehicle, or between designers and the launch site — to someone who can act; and it is closed by fixing it or by flying with it. The first route feeds a learning loop; the second, tentatively, a drift loop. In the informants' accounts, Challenger changed who looks and who decides; tentatively, Columbia changed what counts as enough to fly. We label each proposition as supported, tentative, or our interpretation, and report where the evidence is thin.

## 2. Background

Vaughan's (1996) study of the Challenger launch decision argues that it was "not skullduggery or misconduct but a disastrous mistake": NASA insiders, "when repeatedly faced with evidence that something was wrong, normalized the deviance so that it became acceptable to them" (publisher's description). In Meiksins's (1997) summary, engineers and managers judged the O-rings safe because "a second o-ring would back up the first", and "structural secrecy" made it hard for administrators to know there was a problem. Starbuck and Milliken (1988) describe how "Past successes and acclimatization alter decision-makers' beliefs about probabilities of future success", a fine-tuning that "continues until a serious failure occurs". Vaughan (1990) argues that the effectiveness of NASA's safety regulators was inhibited by the autonomy and interdependence of NASA and its regulators.

The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003) named organizational causes including "reliance on past success as a substitute for sound engineering practices", "organizational barriers that prevented effective communication of critical safety information and stifled professional differences of opinion", "lack of integrated management across program elements", and "mischaracterization of the Shuttle as operational rather than developmental". Mahler (2009) examines NASA's "uneven efforts to institutionalize its own findings" after Challenger.

On voice, Morrison (2014) defines upward voice as communicating "suggestions, concerns, information about problems, or work-related opinions to someone in a higher organizational position". Edmondson (1999) defines team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking". Detert and Burris (2007) find that managerial openness predicts voice, mediated by psychological safety. Morrison and Milliken (2000) treat silence as a "collective-level phenomenon", and Milliken, Morrison and Hewlin (2003) report that employees stay silent mainly for "fear of being viewed or labeled negatively". On learning after failure, Dillon and Tinsley (2008) argue that near-misses — "events in which chance played a role in averting failure" — are read as successes, and Christianson, Farkas, Sutcliffe and Weick (2009) find that rare events "expose weaknesses and reveal unrealized behavioral potential".

As summarized here, these works center on decisions near the moment of failure and on concerns moving up a hierarchy. Following Gioia et al. (2013), we consulted them only after the data structure and model were complete.

## 3. Data and methods

### 3.1 Data

The data are seven oral histories from NASA's STS Recordation Oral History Project, recorded in 2010–2011 by NASA historians (Table 1). From ten candidates we chose seven that cover both accidents and include engineers, managers and one technician; three were screened out because they said little about either accident or belonged to another NASA oral history project. The informants worked on the elements implicated in the accidents — the solid rocket motor and booster, the External Tank and the Orbiter's thermal protection — and on main engine development.

*Table 1. Informants.*

| Informant | Role (as stated in the transcript) | Element | Interviewed | Coded passages |
|:-|:-|:-|:-|-:|
| John W. Thomas | Led NASA's solid rocket motor design team after Challenger; later ASRM program manager | Solid rocket motor | 29 June 2010 | 71 |
| Royce E. Mitchell | Solid rocket motor project manager during the post-Challenger redesign | Solid rocket motor | 30 June 2010 | 120 |
| Gerald W. Smith | Main engine engineer and deputy project manager; Solid Rocket Booster project manager after Challenger | Main engine; booster | 12 May 2011 | 204 |
| Myron A. Pessin | External Tank chief engineer; retired about five years before Columbia | External Tank | 30 June 2010 | 113 |
| Jody A. Singer | Reusable Solid Rocket Motor project manager at the time of Columbia; later Shuttle Propulsion Office deputy | Solid rocket motor | 21 July 2010 | 51 |
| Gerald D. Sheehan | Contractor engineer (Rockwell, later Boeing); Columbia's vehicle manager at KSC, 1979 to mid-1990s | Orbiter | 12 July 2011 | 88 |
| Terrence R. White | Orbiter tile (thermal protection system) technician, later supervisor, at KSC | Orbiter thermal protection | 12 July 2011 | 121 |
| **Total** | | | | **768** |

The transcripts are edited, not verbatim: each is headed "Edited Oral History Transcript" and contains bracketed editorial insertions, which we keep when quoting. Six long bracketed blocks in Mitchell's transcript read as text he added when editing; passages inside them are never counted as first-hand evidence or quoted.

### 3.2 Analysis

The unit of analysis is a *passage*: a stretch of the informant's own speech describing one instance or practice of noticing, raising, escalating, deciding on, deferring or settling a technical problem, or a change in such a practice. Biography, purely technical description, other programs (such as Apollo) and bare answers to an interviewer's yes-or-no question were not coded.

*Open coding* stayed close to the informant's words — a first-order analysis that "tries to adhere faithfully to informant terms" (Gioia et al., 2013) — with no literature terms as codes. It was carried out by AI coding agents (Anthropic's Claude), one per transcript, under written rules with no target number of passages and no example phrases. Every stretch a coder considered and left uncoded was logged with a reason (367 stretches), and every quotation was checked by script against its transcript lines. Each passage was tagged with the period it describes and whether the informant had first-hand knowledge of it. A blind re-tagging of a stratified 10% sample (76 passages) disagreed on 12, of which 5 proved to be errors and were corrected: an estimated error rate of 6.6% in these tags.

*Concepts, themes and dimensions.* The 768 passages were grouped, from their full quotations, into 37 first-order concepts (one primary concept per passage; 227 passages also have a secondary one), each labelled with a first-hand phrase from its own quotations. Concepts were grouped into 15 second-order themes and four aggregate dimensions (Figure 1). This grouping was done by Claude in dialogue with the author, who reviewed and accepted, changed or rejected each decision. Two separate AI analysts, blind to our categories, regrouped the material: at the passage level the adjusted Rand index with ours is 0.28, though 64% of passages fall in a blind group lying mainly within one of our concepts; at the theme level, from labels and definitions alone, agreement was 0.56 for themes and 0.63 for dimensions, with seven of fifteen themes identical. We re-read the quotations behind each disagreement and revised where they supported the blind analyst.

*Grounded model.* We related the themes in 14 propositions (Table 3), each tied to passages belonging to the themes it links, and labelled *supported* (first-hand passages from three or more informants), *tentative*, or *our interpretation*.

*Departures from the method.* Gioia et al. (2013) re-interview informants — "backtrack" — as analysis develops; ours were interviewed by others and cannot be re-asked. They spoke years after the Columbia board's report entered NASA's vocabulary and may retell it. Our procedure is unusually codified; we use it as a check on rigor, not as the "template" or "cookbook" Gioia et al. warn against.

## 4. Findings: the data structure

Figure 1 shows the data structure; Table 2 gives one representative quotation per theme, and the Appendix gives all 51 checked quotations. Four concepts rest on a single informant, and we present them as such: C09, managing what goes up (Smith); C20, giving up margin for weight (Pessin); C26, requirements imposed after Challenger (Mitchell, 11 of 12 passages); and C32, the demand to demonstrate after Columbia (Singer).

![Figure 1. Data structure.](figures/fig1_data_structure.png)

*Figure 1. Data structure. Concept labels are informants' phrases; theme and dimension names are ours.*

**D1. Surfacing problems.** Problems surfaced through handling, testing and flying the hardware (T01); a technician spotted a bad material lot that had passed receiving checks, and the tile shop's rule was “We have to bound it, see how far it goes.” (White, l. 1121–1127). Others stayed out of sight (T02): unannounced supplier changes, failure modes no one understood — “All of us didn’t understand the risk” (Pessin, l. 1406–1410) — and requirements met only on paper, found after Challenger.

**D2. Moving concerns to where they can be acted on.** Concerns crossing organizational lines (T03) moved slowly, were disowned, or were deferred to the other side; booster and tank projects each denied the debris was theirs, and designers left launch-site consequences to “the Cape guys” (Sheehan, l. 1344–1352). Individuals stated their own judgment against the line of authority (T04), often when a senior manager asked for it, at personal cost. Technical depth and proximity let concerns travel (T05).

**D3. Closing technical questions.** Evidence and outside expertise were the main arbiter (T06), within formal channels and decision rights (T07), and committing to fly carried weight (T08). Two routes point in opposite directions. The program flew with problems not fully resolved (T09) — reclassifying them, deciding on incomplete evidence, containing them, or trading margin for weight — or it added protection beyond what the evidence required (T10). Schedule, money and the program's end bore on both (T11).

**D4. Resetting after the accidents.** After Challenger came outside eyes on the solid rocket motor redesign (T12), new people and an effort to end blame between NASA and the contractor (T13), and caution that over-corrected and was pulled back (T14). After Columbia, accepted explanations had to be demonstrated and criteria tightened (T15).

We have to bound it, see how far it goes.” | White, l. 1121–1127 |

## 5. The grounded model

Figure 2 relates the themes over time; Table 3 lists the propositions. The model's claims about change are only as strong as each period's evidence: 290 passages describe the years before Challenger, 261 the Challenger investigation and return to flight, only 41 the years between the accidents, 46 the Columbia investigation and return to flight, 23 the last years of flight, and 107 are undated.

![Figure 2. Grounded model.](figures/fig2_model.png)

*Figure 2. The grounded model. Boxes group the themes of Figure 1; arrow labels are the propositions in Table 3. Solid lines: supported; dashed: tentative; dotted: our interpretation.*

*Table 3. Propositions of the grounded model (full statements in Section 5). Status: supported = first-hand passages from three or more informants; tentative = read as tentative, for the reason given in Section 5; interpretation = the authors' interpretation. Evidence: passages (informants; first-hand).*

| ID | Proposition | Links | Status | Evidence |
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
| P1 | Learning loop | T01 → T06 | supported | 8 (4; 8) |
| P2 | Organizational lines divert concerns | T03 → T09 | supported | 10 (4; 10) |
| P3 | Drift loop | T09 → T02 | tentative | 7 (3; 1) |
| P4 | Pressure pushes closure ahead of evidence | T11 → T06, T09, T02 | supported | 9 (4; 9) |
| P5 | Depth and proximity speed concerns toward closure | T05 → T03, T06 | supported | 10 (5; 10) |
| P6 | Individual judgment reaches the decision when asked for | T04 → T07 | supported | 10 (3; 10) |
| P7 | Challenger: outside eyes push closure toward evidence and protection | T12 → T06, T10 | supported | 12 (3; 12) |
| P8 | Challenger: new people and a new contractor relationship | T13 → T03, T05 | supported | 7 (3; 7) |
| P9 | Challenger: over-correction, then pull-back | T14 → T07 | supported | 11 (3; 11) |
| P10 | Challenger sharpened the weight of committing to fly | T12, T13 → T08 | supported | 7 (3; 7) |
| P11 | Challenger's reset stayed close to the failed element | T14 → T09, T03 | tentative | 8 (3; 5) |
| P12 | Columbia changed the standard of proof | T15 → T06, T07, T02 | tentative | 9 (2; 8) |
| P13 | The end of the program steered closure toward containment | T11 → T09, T10 | tentative | 7 (2; 6) |
| P14 | Who looks and decides versus what counts as enough | T12, T14 → T15 | interpretation | 7 (5; 7) |

**The cycle.** In the learning loop (P1, supported), problems surfacing in the hardware are chased to a cause, fixed, and checked across the fleet — a weak tile on one orbiter led the shop to check the others (White, l. 741–749). In the drift loop (P3, tentative), accommodating a known problem — treating it as maintenance, explaining it away, or trusting a second seal — keeps it in service and out of view as a safety issue: foam loss “was always a refurbish issue for the orbiter” (Pessin, l. 1437–1441). Pessin's account of the program declining to open an in-flight anomaly two flights before Columbia (Pessin, l. 1443–1451) is second-hand, as is most of P3's evidence (six of seven passages), and all of it is told in hindsight about the problems that later caused accidents. White's account of repair criteria relaxed after a flight went better than feared (White, l. 1241–1243) is counter-evidence: the same mechanism, presented as learning, with no later harm.

**Conditions.** Concerns whose cause and effect sit in different organizations move slowly or are disowned, and tend to end in negotiation or accommodation rather than evidence (P2, supported) — though in the icing case an improvised test helped settle the dispute. Schedule and budget pressure push teams to commit hardware before test results and cut instrumentation that would have made problems visible (P4, supported; Smith, l. 263–277). Technical depth and proximity speed concerns toward closure (P5, supported), a claim made mostly by those who built these arrangements. Individual judgment changes a decision mainly when a senior person asks for it or the individual holds data the decision-maker lacks, at a personal cost (P6, supported); Smith supplies half of this evidence.

**What Challenger changed.** Outside reviewers pushed closure in the redesigned motor toward test evidence and toward protection beyond what the team's tests required, such as joint heaters Thomas judged unnecessary (Thomas, l. 782–786; P7). New leaders came in, NASA moved its team into the contractor's plant, and NASA managers worked to stop the blame (P8), though Smith describes a strained relationship with the contractor's program manager. The swing to caution flooded formal channels — thousands of review item discrepancies (Smith, l. 1706–1712) — until managers restored pace and the tile shop won back standard repairs (P9). Committing to fly felt heavier for those who flew the redesigned hardware (P10). All four are supported, but only by the solid rocket motor team and, for P9, White. Tentatively (P11), the reset stayed close to the failed element: other elements saw procedural tightening and more documentation, and between the accidents debris crossing element lines was still argued over and accommodated (Smith, l. 1800–1808). The link between these halves is our inference, the between-accident evidence is thin, and the passages on the path to Columbia are second-hand.

**What Columbia and the program's end changed.** Tentatively (P12), Columbia changed the standard of proof: engineers gained latitude to question inherited explanations, risk was presented in more detail, and criteria and in-flight imaging tightened. This rests on Singer and White only; no informant decided for the External Tank or the program at the time. Tentatively (P13), late in the program the time a change took to reach the hardware pushed decisions toward continued flight with extra inspection, with changes reserved for safety (Singer, l. 812–826) — almost entirely Singer's account.

**Our interpretation (P14).** Read together, Challenger mainly changed *who looks at a problem and who decides*; Columbia mainly changed *what counts as enough to fly*. No informant states this; White alone gives first-hand accounts of both resets.

## 6. Discussion

The drift loop resembles normalization of deviance as summarized for Vaughan (1996) and the board's "reliance on past success as a substitute for sound engineering practices" (CAIB, 2003). Our data add a distinction: accommodation that later proved dangerous sits beside accommodation that did not. Dillon and Tinsley's (2008) near-miss concept suggests asking whether the evidence that a problem was tolerable came from chance. Given P3's status, this is a direction for research, not a finding.

The voice works summarized above concern upward voice and team-level safety. Our informants place most delays at organizational boundaries — contractor to program, element to element, design to launch site — which a team-level construct does not capture, although P6 fits Detert and Burris's (2007) finding on managerial openness. The data also show voice built into procedure, and after Challenger that formal voice multiplying until it clogged closure (P9); whether this is recognized in the fuller literature should be checked before it is claimed as a contribution.

The accident dimension fits Christianson et al.'s (2009) account of rare events, while tentative P11 suggests the learning stayed close to the failed element, consistent with Mahler's (2009) "uneven efforts to institutionalize its own findings". As transferable concepts (Gioia et al., 2013) we offer the two-loop cycle, organizational lines as a condition that diverts concerns from evidence to negotiation, and — as our interpretation — the idea that failures may reset different parts of the cycle.

## 7. Limitations

*Sample.* Seven informants cannot speak for the program. None is from Thiokol, and none decided for the External Tank or the program at the time of Columbia; White is a technician and supervisor, and Sheehan worked for a contractor.

*Data.* The oral histories were recorded by others, years after both accidents, and could not be followed up; informants may retell the Columbia board's account. The transcripts are edited, and Mitchell's added passages are excluded from first-hand evidence. Only 41 of 768 passages describe the years between the accidents.

*Evidence.* P3, P11, P12 and P13 are tentative: P3 and P11's path to Columbia rest largely on second-hand, hindsight accounts, and P12 and P13 on one or two informants. P14 is our interpretation. Four concepts rest on a single informant: C09 (Smith), C20 (Pessin), C26 (Mitchell) and C32 (Singer).

*Coding.* The era and first-hand tags have an estimated 6.6% error rate. Open coding was done by AI agents and grouping by an AI analyst under the author's review; blind regroupings agreed only partly (0.28 for passages; 0.56 for themes, 0.63 for dimensions).

*Literature.* We did not read the full texts of Vaughan (1996) or Edmondson (1999); our claims about them rest on the publisher's description, the published abstract and Meiksins's (1997) review. Other works are cited only for their abstracts, and the CAIB report for its Executive Summary. Works verified only by bibliographic details are not cited.
